title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The run used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) to respect the model‑call budget; executed model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have used ≈400). Results (adversarial cluster reported): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) could not be meaningfully evaluated in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial injection calibration, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed as intent→configuration translators in NetOps because they can reduce operator effort and speed routine changes. However, erroneous or misordered device changes can cause outage, policy violation, or security exposure. A common mitigation is to pair an LLM with deterministic validators or sandboxed simulators in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so that any proposed configuration is checked before execution. Motivated by this architecture and by calls in recent surveys and prototypes for reproducible, workflow‑centred evaluations of agentic NetOps systems, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment that aimed to measure whether deterministic verifier augmentation causally reduces verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from an LLM under both benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistered estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline) tested by an exact McNemar two‑sided test with paired bootstrap CIs. The run used synthetic deterministic topologies and an explicit paired design (N=200 tasks). The principal, archived outcome was that every sampled LLM candidate was labeled SAFE by the deterministic verifier in both arms; this ceiling outcome rendered the preregistered causal test non‑informative. Rather than attempting to overturn that factual outcome, the rest of the paper: (1) documents the confirmatory design choices and exact numerical results obtained; (2) provides an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the execution was non‑informative for the intended estimand; and (3) gives concrete, archive‑supported design recommendations to make informative repeats feasible.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and prototype reports establish the rapid uptake of LLMs in NetOps tasks such as intent translation, configuration synthesis, and limited remediation; they also emphasize safety concerns when models output executable changes (surveys and prototypes, 2025–2026). Architecturally, a recurring pattern is tool‑augmentation (LLM + external deterministic tools such as validators or simulators) and generate–validate–refine pipelines; empirical reports show these pipelines can reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks but that effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity and evaluation semantics. Work on guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and agent orchestration stresses trade‑offs: strict validators can lower unsafe acceptance but may increase false refusals or operator workload and must be stress‑tested with adversarial templates. Evaluation methodology literature for agentic NetOps advocates workflow‑centred, replayable, sandboxed experiments that record initial/final states and deterministic validator traces; our design follows these desiderata and addresses a literature gap: reproducible, preregistered adversarial NetOps experiments that quantify the paired causal effect of adding a deterministic verifier under transparent generation semantics are rare.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where each arm yields a binary SAFE indicator from a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; CIs: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples; seed = 1729). Planned paired episodes: 200 tasks × 2 arms = 200 paired trials. Power: preregistered to detect an approximate 7 percentage‑point paired reduction (assumed baseline unsafe ≈10–15%) with 80% power, hence N=200.

Task generator, scope, and seeds. A deterministic generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS multi‑device topologies and to configuration fields {admin, mtu, vlan}. Each task manifest included initial_state, expected_final_state, a required_sequence (workflow policy), and difficulty metadata; generator seeds were deterministic and archived. Tasks were clustered into benign and adversarial variants via a preregistered obfuscation template set intended to raise adversarial difficulty; those templates and the generator code were frozen in the preregistration.

Pipelines compared and scoring. Baseline: LLM candidate accepted and scored post hoc by the deterministic validator. Guarded: same LLM candidate validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 running in a sandbox; the validator emitted deterministic structured traces (validation_before/after, violation lists). The preregistration allowed an optional single repair call in the guarded arm, but for the confirmatory episodes no repairs were applied (repair traces are null), so guarded here reflects pure validation rather than repair‑driven changes. Confirmatory binary outcomes derive from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE).

Generation semantics and budget. Two generation semantics were preregistered: independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task) and shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task scored by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve the hosted model budget; executed model_calls_used = 200 while independent per‑arm generation would have required ≈400 calls. This choice reduces per‑arm stochastic variation and therefore reduces the opportunity for discordant paired outcomes unless repairs or nondeterministic validators intervene.

Analysis. The deterministic validator outputs were analyzed via a preregistered paired_binary_analysis executor. We produced the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples; seed = 1729). Missingness and exclusion rules were applied per the preregistration (automatic retries, deterministic duplication checks, nondeterminism flags). All actions and parameter choices were logged and archived so numerical outputs can be reproduced deterministically from the archived bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The confirmatory run completed 400 episodes (200 paired episodes) with zero technical failures and model_calls_used = 200 under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Provider auditing recorded 200 completed hosted model calls and no cache reuse across arms. No contaminated or nondeterministic tasks were observed in the confirmatory set; the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. Paired contingency counts: n11 = 200; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. From these counts the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; seed = 1729). Representative validator traces show validation_before and validation_after with violation_count = 0 and valid = true for sampled tasks; repair_provider_trace entries are null for all confirmatory episodes, confirming that no repairs were invoked.

Diagnostic note on testability. McNemar‑style paired inference requires discordant pairs (n10 or n01) to evaluate arm differences; the observed ceiling (n11 = 200) yields a degenerate estimate and p = 1.0. This degeneracy reflects the conjunction of (1) shared generation semantics (one identical candidate per task shared by both arms), (2) a deterministic validator that labeled every candidate SAFE, and (3) absence of repair‑induced candidate changes. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (~10–15%) and discordant proportions; those assumptions were not met, so the confirmatory hypothesis was not testable in this execution.
sections.discussion:
Root‑cause synthesis. The degenerate contingency arises from the executed design choices and observed validator outputs. Because both arms scored the same generated candidate and no repairs or validator nondeterminism produced per‑arm differences, there was no possible mechanism for discordant paired outcomes. The model_call arithmetic in the preregistration makes the trade‑off explicit: independent per‑arm generation would have doubled model calls (≈400 total) and restored an opportunity for arm‑level stochasticity to produce discordance; shared generation saved calls at the cost of testability when baseline unsafe rate was near zero.

Design recommendations (artifact‑grounded). All recommendations follow from archived facts and should be preregistered before repeats: (1) use independent per‑arm generation for a paired causal contrast unless the guarded arm reliably applies deterministic repairs that produce candidate differences; (2) consume a preregistered exploratory reserve (we reserved up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial templates until the baseline unsafe rate meets the power assumptions, then freeze those transforms in the preregistration; (3) if repairs are enabled, archive repair_provider_trace artifacts and quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and any repair‑introduced violations; (4) perform a deterministic pilot check on a small holdout to detect ceiling/floor contingencies and, if observed, follow preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptation paths (e.g., enable independent draws or strengthen adversarial injections) rather than proceeding with an uninformative confirmatory test.

Alternative estimands. When budget constraints preclude independent per‑arm draws, a different preregistered estimand remains testable under shared semantics: estimate the single‑arm absolute unsafe‑proposal rate (with CIs), or treat the guarded pipeline as a refusal gate and estimate refusal and post‑repair SAFE rates (requires repairs). These alternative estimands shift resource needs but preserve inferential validity; they were enumerated as secondary/exploratory options in the preregistration.

Threats to validity and externality. Internal validity: the major internal limitation here is generation semantics—shared draws removed per‑arm stochasticity. Construct validity: the synthetic task family limited fields (admin/mtu/vlan) and topology types; the validator implements full_intent_constraint_validation for that family but may not cover production failure modes. External validity: results use a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic topologies; generalization to multi‑vendor, multi‑AS, or real operational datasets is not claimed. Conclusion validity: the absence of discordant pairs prevents any inferential claim about verifier efficacy; the artifacts instead support methodological conclusions about testability and resource budgeting.

Operational implications. Teams must balance model‑call budgets against the need for per‑arm independence when designing paired causal tests. For deployment, guardrails can reduce risk but may introduce false refusals and operator workload; our confirmatory run cannot quantify that trade‑off because no refusals occurred. The preregistered exploratory reserve was intended to estimate ROC/refusal characteristics and should be consumed during pilot calibration in future repeats.

Reproducibility. All execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts (task generator, shared responses, scoring JSONs, contingency tables, bootstrap parameters) are archived in the supplied execution bundle and permit deterministic replay of the identical non‑informative outcome. Readers and auditors can replay the exact run to confirm the arithmetic and diagnostic conclusions; full artifact pointers and checksums are maintained in the archive and summarized in the Disclosure Statement so that the main text remains focused on scientific interpretation rather than manifest enumeration.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that adding the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run archived for deterministic replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the exploratory reserve, and pilot contingency checks) to enable informative repeats. We urge future preregistered repeats to align generation semantics, adversarial calibration, and model‑call budgeting with the intended estimand so that paired causal contrasts become testable.

Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals and tooling were developed pre‑lock but were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under the post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic task scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS multi‑device setups and to fields {admin, mtu, vlan}; results may not generalize to production multi‑vendor or multi‑AS contexts.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when sampled candidates were valid.

Adversarial calibration: the preregistered adversarial templates in the executed run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial injections or consuming the exploratory reserve are required to produce informative discordance under the paired estimand.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; we do not claim multi‑model generality.

Validator completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 was run in a synthetic sandbox and may not capture the full breadth of production failure modes; external validation of validator completeness is needed for production extrapolation.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor field trials were performed; operator burden and false‑refusal trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
